questions.q: In the Doverfield case study, why is 'system of record' decided per data domain rather than per object?
options: Because a single object like Account can have some fields owned by the ERP and other fields owned by Salesforce, so the ownership decision has to be made field by field, not for the whole object at once
Because Salesforce objects cannot hold ERP data under any circumstances
Because ERPs do not support the concept of a system of record
Because every field on every object must always be owned by Salesforce
questions.explain: Doverfield's Account record is shared: the ERP originates product/pricing/inventory data while Salesforce originates relationship and pipeline data, even on overlapping objects -- which is why the ownership matrix has to be built field by field.

questions.q: Which sync pattern does Doverfield use when a rep needs to check live inventory before committing a quantity on a quote?
options: Batch integration
Event-driven integration
Real-time request-reply
No integration is needed for this case
questions.explain: A rep needing an answer immediately, in the same interaction, is exactly what a synchronous request-reply callout is for -- the Apex transaction waits for the ERP's answer before continuing.

questions.q: Why does Doverfield use an event-driven pattern, rather than request-reply, to create a sales order in the ERP when an Opportunity closes?
options: Because order creation needs to be reliable but doesn't need to block or slow down the transaction that closed the deal in Salesforce
Because event-driven integration is always faster than request-reply
Because the ERP cannot accept synchronous callouts
Because Platform Events are required for all integrations regardless of use case
questions.explain: Closing the deal shouldn't wait on the ERP's response -- firing a Platform Event decouples the reliable-but-not-instant order creation from the user's immediate close action.

questions.q: What specific problem does marking a field as an External ID and using it with upsert solve?
options: It lets a sync job reliably insert-or-update the correct record using the other system's own key, without first querying to determine which case applies
It automatically encrypts the field's contents
It prevents the field from ever being edited by a user
It converts the field into a formula field
questions.explain: External ID plus upsert is specifically what lets a sync avoid a separate query-then-decide step, using the other system's key directly to find or create the right record.

questions.q: Why is matching ERP customer records to Salesforce Accounts on Account Name a risky design choice, per this lesson?
options: Account Name is not a valid Salesforce field type
Names can change, contain typos, or collide between different real customers, causing a sync built on them to create duplicate records instead of updating the correct one
Account Name fields cannot be included in Bulk API jobs
ERPs never store a customer name field at all
questions.explain: A human-readable field like a name is not a reliable, stable key -- the lesson calls this out as a common, expensive mistake that an External ID matched on the ERP's own stable key avoids.
